tip: A modal like 'mag' pairs with a main verb that goes to the very end: mag ik binnenkomen (may I come in).
'je' is the informal you for friends and family, as in ik kom je ophalen. Switch to 'u' with strangers or elders.
'u' is the polite you for strangers and formal settings: kennis met u te maken (pleased to meet you).
Modern Dutch leans toward 'je' even with strangers, as in ik zie je weer, but default to 'u' in service, writing, or with elders.
'dat' (that) sends the verb to the clause end: dat hij gelijk heeft, with 'heeft' landing last.
Use 'geen' to negate a noun with no article: geen broers of zussen (no brothers or sisters). 'niet' negates everything else.
The prefix 'schoon-' turns a family word into the in-law version: schoonmoeder (mother-in-law), schoonvader, schoonzus.
Open with a time word and the verb still comes second, subject after it: Gisteren kocht zij (yesterday bought she).
The perfect uses hebben plus a participle that lands at the end: ik heb je gemist (I have missed you).
'gaan' plus an infinitive expresses the near future, like English 'going to': ik ga boodschappen doen (I'm going to shop).
Overstappen is separable: the prefix 'over' breaks off and moves down the sentence, as in ik stap over op een andere lijn.
For change-of-state verbs Dutch builds the perfect with 'zijn', not hebben: ik ben geboren (I was born).
Where English says 'no X', Dutch uses 'geen X': geen idee (no idea). For 'not X' with a verb or adjective, use 'niet'.
'er' is a dummy subject for 'there is/are' and is not translated: Er staan vijfduizend bomen (there stand five thousand trees).
'een appeltje te schillen' literally means a little apple to peel, the Dutch way of saying a bone to pick.
'je/jij' is the informal you for friends and peers, as in Kun je; switch to 'u' for strangers, elders, or business.
Open with an adverb and Dutch puts the verb before the subject: Gelukkig kwam de bus (fortunately came the bus), unlike English.
Yes/no questions just put the verb first, with no 'do' helper: Spreekt u Engels? (speak you English?).
Front a phrase and the verb stays second, ahead of the subject: Na de les gaan de studenten (after the class go the students).
Motion toward a destination takes 'zijn', not hebben, where English uses 'have': zijn naar het strand gerend (ran to the beach).
'hoeven' pushes the main verb to the clause end: niet vandaag af te hebben (doesn't have to be finished today).
'er' is a dummy subject in there-is/there-are sentences and is not translated: Er is geen melk (there is no milk).
Comparisons use 'dan' for 'than': groter dan (taller than). Learners often say 'groter als' by mistake, but standard Dutch is 'dan'.
'doordat' means because for a direct cause or result, often unintended, while 'omdat' gives a reason or motive: Doordat zij te laat vertrok (because she left too late).
'de gebeten hond' literally means the bitten dog, the Dutch image for the one everyone blames or who takes the fall.
'hoe' plus a comparative twice means 'the more... the more': hoe langer... hoe meer (the longer... the more).
Put a phrase first and the verb comes second, so the subject follows it: Behalve op vrijdag heeft het museum (except Friday has the museum).
'of' here means whether and drives the whole verb cluster to the clause end: of wij mee willen gaan (whether we want to come along).
'worden' plus a participle is the passive, and 'door' marks the doer: wordt bezorgd door de koerier (is delivered by the courier).
In an 'als' clause the verb goes last (is), but the main clause keeps the verb second: Als het mooi weer is, gaan wij (if the weather is nice, go we).
The imperative is just the verb stem: Zet (turn down). Add 'u' for formal (Zet u) or 'laten we' for let's.
'omdat' and 'want' both mean because, but 'omdat' sends the verb to the clause end while 'want' keeps normal order: omdat het hard regent (because it is raining hard).
'worden' marks the ongoing or future action (zal worden bezorgd, will be delivered) while 'zijn' marks the finished state (is verstuurd, has been sent).
'Ik wil' can sound blunt, so soften a request with 'Ik zou graag ... willen': Ik zou graag meer willen weten (I would like to know more).
Dutch opens a subjectless passive with 'er', naming no agent: er worden veel fietsen gestolen (many bikes get stolen).
A bare number needs 'er' meaning 'of them': ik heb er vijf nodig (I need five of them).
Prepositional 'er' splits from its preposition when a word sits between: ik denk er vaak aan (I often think about it), with 'vaak' wrapped inside.
In a question 'zullen we...?' means 'shall we...?', a suggestion, not just the future: zullen we samen gaan (shall we go together).
'te' plus an adjective plus 'om ... te' means 'too ... to': te moe om ... te gaan (too tired to go).
A sentence-final 'hè' is a tag meaning 'right?' or 'isn't it?', seeking agreement: lekker weertje, hè? (nice weather, right?).
'ondanks' takes a noun, not a full clause: ondanks de vertraging (despite the delay). For a clause use 'hoewel' or 'ondanks dat'.
Purpose wraps the infinitive in 'om ... te' meaning 'in order to': om te studeren (in order to study), with 'te' just before the verb.
Front an adverb like 'desondanks' and the verb jumps ahead of the subject: Desondanks bleef hij (nevertheless remained he), not hij bleef.
'vergeten' takes a plain 'te' with no 'om': de deur op slot te doen (to lock the door). Some other verbs add 'om te' instead.
Put 'het' before an infinitive to turn a verb into a noun: het opruimen (the cleaning-up), so begonnen met het opruimen means started the tidying.
'krijgen te horen' literally means to get to hear, the Dutch way of saying to be told: kregen te horen dat (were told that).
